opus-5.5.text:
I think it's become a lot less important than people assume, honestly. A few years ago, if you wanted to build something useful with language models, you basically needed people who understood the architecture deeply, who could fine-tune, who knew what was happening inside the model. That's just not the case anymore for most applications.

The models have gotten good enough, and the interfaces around them have matured enough, that the bottleneck has shifted. What really matters now is understanding your problem and your users. Can you figure out what the workflow actually is? Can you get access to the right data and plug the model into the systems where the work happens? Can you build good evaluation so you know whether the thing is working? That's product and engineering expertise, plus domain knowledge, much more than ML research expertise.

There's still a place for deep expertise, though. If you're doing something at the frontier, or you need to customize a model heavily for a specialized domain, or you care a lot about cost and latency at scale, then having people who really understand the models pays off. They know when to fine-tune versus when to prompt, how to set up retrieval properly, and how to diagnose failures. That intuition is valuable.

But for the median team building an AI application, I'd say: don't block on hiring a bunch of PhDs. Hire strong engineers who are curious and willing to learn, find people who deeply understand the problem you're solving, and lean on the model providers for the heavy lifting on the model itself. That's part of what we're trying to do at Cohere: absorb as much of that complexity as possible so companies can focus on building the thing that actually creates value for them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says deep language-model expertise is unnecessary for most application teams and emphasizes product, engineering, and domain knowledge. It does not claim that teams building the best AI products need deep familiarity with how to build language models.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it matters a lot less than people assume, and I'd argue it's becoming less important every year. When we started Cohere, the premise was basically that most companies shouldn't need to hire a team of researchers who understand transformers at the architecture level in order to build something useful. That should be our job. The model should be a capable thing you can pick up and use, the same way you don't need to understand how a database engine implements B-trees to build a product on Postgres.

What I do think teams need is a kind of practical intuition about these systems. How do they fail? When do they hallucinate? What does it mean to give the model the right context versus asking it to recall something from training? How do you evaluate whether it's actually working on your problem, rather than just looking impressive in a demo? That's a very different skill set from being able to derive attention from first principles. It's closer to good product engineering, and I'd honestly rather have a team with deep expertise in their own domain, whether that's healthcare or finance or legal, than one with deep expertise in language models and no idea what the customer actually needs.

Where the deep expertise still matters is at the frontier. If you're training models, if you're pushing on fine-tuning, retrieval, tool use, the things that determine whether the model is reliable enough for an enterprise to trust it, then yes, you need people who really understand what's happening under the hood. But that's a relatively small number of organizations, and I think the whole industry's job is to shrink the gap so that the enormous number of companies who just want to deploy this stuff can do so without having to become AI labs themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says deep language-model expertise matters for frontier work such as training models and improving reliability, but it does not say that teams building the best AI products have that expertise.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you’re building, but for most application teams, deep language-model expertise isn’t the main thing you need. You need to understand the problem you’re solving and what a good result looks like for your users.

You do need practical familiarity with the models: where they’re useful, where they fail, and how to evaluate them on your particular task. But that’s different from knowing how to train one from scratch. A team that understands a workflow really well and can reliably measure whether its product improves that workflow can build something valuable without being a team of language-model researchers.

r001.rationale: The response says deep language-model expertise is not the main need for most application teams and distinguishes practical familiarity from knowing how to train models. It does not say the best AI products come from teams deeply familiar with building language models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you’re building. If you’re training models, that expertise is essential. But if you’re building an application on top of them, you shouldn’t need a team of researchers to make something useful.

You do need to understand how the models behave: where they’re reliable, where they fail, and how to evaluate them for your particular use case. But often the harder problem is understanding the customer’s workflow. What are they trying to accomplish? What information does the model need? How do you know whether it actually helped?

So I’d put a lot of weight on domain expertise and strong engineering. Someone who understands the problem deeply and can build a good feedback loop can get a long way without knowing every detail of how the model was trained.

r001.rationale: The response says deep expertise is essential for training models, but application teams can build useful products without knowing the details of model training. It does not say the best AI products require teams with deep familiarity with building language models.
